opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was really a practical decision more than anything else. When we were doing the user study, we had over a thousand artists who wanted to participate, and the logistics of having every single one of them upload their own portfolio, run it through the tool, wait for it to process, and then fine-tune a model on their specific style to see the mimicry results, that just wasn't feasible at the time. Each of those mimicry experiments takes real compute and real time, and we were a small academic lab trying to move quickly because artists were being harmed right then.

And there's also a privacy and trust dimension to it. A lot of artists, understandably, were very wary of uploading their work anywhere, especially to a research group they'd never heard of, in the context of AI. The whole reason they came to us was that their work was being taken without consent. So asking them to hand over their art so we could train models on it felt like the wrong thing to do.

So what we did instead was pick a representative set of artists and styles covering a broad range: different media, painting, illustration, line art, more realistic versus more stylized work. We applied Glaze, ran mimicry attacks with and without protection, and showed participants the outputs side by side. Artists are actually the best judges here. They know immediately whether something captures a style or not, often far better than any automated metric like CLIP scores. So having them evaluate those representative examples gave us a really strong signal about whether the protection was working and whether the perturbations were acceptable visually, without putting anyone's own work at risk in the process.

r001.rationale: The response says artists judged representative examples and their visual effects, but does not state that they could mentally project those effects onto their own art.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so that's a great question, and it's one we actually spent a lot of time thinking about. The honest answer is that at the time we ran the user study, Glaze was still a research prototype. It was slow, it was running on our own servers, and it was nowhere near something we could just hand to a thousand people and say, "go upload your portfolio and tell us what you think." The compute cost alone would have been prohibitive, and the turnaround per image was on the order of many minutes on a GPU.

But the more important reason is methodological. If you let everyone upload their own art, you lose control over the experiment. Every artist has a different style, a different medium, a different sensitivity to what counts as a visible artifact. Some artists do very clean line work where even tiny perturbations might jump out, and others work in heavily textured oil painting styles where you could hide a lot. So if person A says "this looks fine" and person B says "this is ruined," you don't actually know whether that's the protection behaving differently or just two people with very different thresholds looking at very different images. By giving everyone the same curated set of examples, across a range of styles and across different intensity levels of the perturbation, we could actually compare responses. We could say, at this intensity, this percentage of artists found it acceptable, and we knew everyone was reacting to the same thing.

The other piece is that the evaluation wasn't just "does this look okay to you." We also needed to show them what the mimicry results looked like, so they could judge whether the protection was actually working. That meant we had to go train the style mimicry models ourselves, on protected and unprotected versions of the same artwork, and show them side by side. You can't do that in real time for every participant. That's hours of training per artist. So the representative set let us do the full pipeline, protection, then attack, then outcome, and present the whole picture to artists so they could make an informed trade-off judgment.

And I'll say, we did work very closely with artists throughout. Karla Ortiz and others were involved from the beginning, and the examples we chose were vetted by artists, not just by us picking what we thought looked good. We were very conscious of the fact that we're computer scientists, we're not artists, and our eyes are not trained the way theirs are. So the representative-sample approach was really about letting the artists' expertise speak in a controlled way, rather than us assuming we knew what "imperceptible" meant.

Now, once we released the tool publicly, that's when the real test happened. Thousands of artists downloaded it, ran it on their own work, and we got an enormous amount of feedback, some of it quite critical about artifacts on certain styles. And that was invaluable, that fed directly into the subsequent versions. So in a sense we did eventually do the "everyone tests their own art" evaluation, it just came after the controlled study rather than instead of it.

r001.rationale: The response says representative examples let artists compare responses across styles and judge trade-offs, but it does not state that they could mentally project Glaze’s visible effects onto their own art.

astra-6.text:
We wanted artists to understand the tradeoff we were asking them to evaluate: how much Glaze might visibly change an image, and whether that change would be acceptable to them as a way to protect their work. Showing representative examples gave everyone a common basis for that judgment.

Having each person upload their own art would have made it a different kind of study, with more setup and more variability. The limitation, of course, is that looking at someone else’s artwork isn’t the same as looking at your own. An artist may notice changes in their own work that another person would miss. So those responses give us useful feedback, but they don’t establish that every artist would be comfortable with the results on every piece.

r001.rationale: The response says representative examples gave artists a common basis for judging visible changes, but it does not state that they could mentally project those effects onto their own art. It instead notes that viewing someone else’s artwork is not the same as viewing one’s own.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted artists to have a consistent basis for judging the results. If everyone uploaded their own work, differences in style, subject matter, and the images they chose would make their reactions hard to compare. Showing representative examples let us ask a more focused question: Is the visual change introduced by Glaze acceptable to you as an artist? That’s different from asking whether it works well on every individual’s portfolio, which would require a much broader evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response says representative examples made reactions easier to compare, but it does not state that artists could mentally project Glaze’s visible effects onto their own art.
